clue.text: Go over the plot — I'm hard to please

parts.note: to cross something is to go over it
a patch is a small plot of ground, as in a vegetable patch

explanation.surface: Someone sulkily refusing to be satisfied by a story's plot, or by a garden.
explanation.walkthrough: The dash makes the second half sound like a speaker's confession; it is the definition, written in the first person.
explanation.definitionFit: A crosspatch is a bad-tempered, grumpy person who is difficult to satisfy.

clue.text: This chap's on Ben's side, possibly

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a steep rock face, perhaps on a mountain

explanation.surface: A man who sides with his friend Ben.
explanation.walkthrough: Ben looks like a friend's name; in Scotland a ben is a mountain, and one of its sides could be a sheer rock face.
explanation.definitionFit: Cliff is a man's first name, and also a steep rock face such as a mountain flank.

clue.text: Sick of company tucking into meal?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: tucking into means getting inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: meal is ground grain, like flour
CO is the abbreviation for company

explanation.surface: Feeling ill from all the company tucking into a big dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sick of' reads as fed up with; 'of' actually goes into the answer, and 'meal' is ground grain, not dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Off colour is an idiom for slightly unwell or not in good health.

clue.text: Don't run off before hearing its report

definitions.text: Don't run off before hearing its report

parts.words: Don't run off before hearing its report
parts.note: surface reading: stay put until you've heard the account or the news
setter's reading: report is the bang of a gun that sets runners going in a race

explanation.surface: Advice not to leave before a document is read out.
explanation.walkthrough: A gun's report is its bang; sprinters must not set off before the bang, or it is a false start.
explanation.definitionFit: The gun fired to begin a race gives athletes the signal to go.

clue.text: A graduate goes around Viking territory overseas

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: goes around means encircles, so one piece is put outside the other

parts.note: MA is a Master of Arts, a graduate
Eric the Red was a famous Viking

explanation.surface: A graduate travels round the lands the Vikings settled abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: Eric the Red founded Norse Greenland, and his son reached North America, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: America lies across the Atlantic, so from Britain it is a land beyond the sea.

clue.text: Offer admission for a charge

parts.note: surface reading: let people in for an entrance fee
setter's reading: an admission of guilt, made in respect of a criminal accusation

explanation.surface: A venue letting visitors in on payment of a fee.
explanation.walkthrough: Admission and charge both suggest tickets and fees; here they are an admission of guilt and a criminal charge.
explanation.definitionFit: To confess is to own up to wrongdoing, as an accused person may do to an offence.

clue.text: Some columns, to Athenians

indicators.note: some of the following letters are taken, so the answer sits within the run of words

parts.note: the end of columns joins the start of to Athenians

explanation.surface: How Greek columns were described by the ancient people of Athens.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the definition and the wordplay: 'Some' signals that only some letters are taken, and the Athenian touch fits, since a stoa is Greek.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoa is a covered colonnade or portico in ancient Greek architecture, a row of pillars.

clue.text: Traditional outdoor type of carriage parking

parts.note: a tram is a passenger carriage on rails
P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned, open-air kind of vehicle parking.
explanation.definitionFit: A tramp is a homeless wanderer, long pictured sleeping under hedges in the open air.

clue.text: Relying on hearsay can lead to error

indicators.note: an error puts things wrong, so these letters end up out of their order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A warning that trusting rumour can produce mistakes.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as a true moral; 'error' is the anagram signal, at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Anecdotal evidence rests on personal stories rather than proof, so it depends on second-hand reports.

clue.text: Circus performer the second person retracting?

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for second
someone taking back what they said swallows their words

explanation.surface: A circus act described as the second person backing out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second person' looks like the grammar term 'you'; second gives S alone, and the person retracting is one who eats their words.
explanation.definitionFit: This performer lowers a blade down the throat as a circus or sideshow act.

clue.text: Use an airline in the process of expansion?

definitions.text: Use an airline in the process of expansion?

parts.note: surface reading: book a seat with an air carrier
setter's reading: work an air line, the hose at a garage, to pump up a tyre

explanation.surface: Taking a flight with a company that is busy growing its business.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'airline' as two words, an air line: the hose at a filling station used to blow up tyres.
explanation.definitionFit: To pump air into a tyre or balloon makes it swell, which is exactly expansion.

clue.text: Deny ringing women's prison

indicators.note: ringing means encircling, so one piece is put around the other

parts.note: to negate is to deny
W is the standard abbreviation for women

explanation.surface: Officials deny that anyone has been phoning a women's jail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'women's prison' reads as one phrase, but women's only gives W; Newgate was the notorious old London prison.
explanation.definitionFit: Newgate was a famous London jail, demolished in 1904, so the name stands for a particular prison.

clue.text: Harmful effect of cold — best for it to be treated

indicators.note: treated means worked on or processed, so these letters are reworked

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Medical advice that a chill is best dealt with promptly.
explanation.walkthrough: The medical surface makes 'treated' look like care for the patient; it is the anagram signal, and 'for it' is fodder too.
explanation.definitionFit: Frostbite is tissue damage to fingers, toes or nose caused by freezing temperatures.

clue.text: Bound to be embarrassed about shortage of work?

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: an embarrassed face goes red
op is the short form of opus, a work

explanation.surface: Someone sure to feel ashamed at being out of a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortage of work' suggests unemployment; it means the shortened form of work, OP from opus. 'Bound to be' reads as 'certain to be'.
explanation.definitionFit: Roped means tied up with rope, so the past participle matches bound in the sense of tied.

clue.text: Fruit of tree -a trick to snare first of race?

indicators.note: to snare is to trap, so one piece catches the other inside it

parts.note: a plus con, a trick or swindle

indicators.note: first of asks for only the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: the opening letter of race

explanation.surface: A tree's fruit used as bait to trap the leader of a race.
explanation.definitionFit: An acorn is the nut borne by the oak, so it is literally a tree's fruit.

clue.text: A very old port I got out for The Queen"

indicators.note: got out means removed or ejected, so the named letter leaves the word

parts.note: the ancient Egyptian harbour city founded by Alexander
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone bringing out an aged wine to toast the monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very old port' suggests a vintage wine to drink the Queen's health; it is the ancient city.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexandra was queen consort to Edward VII, so the name fits a queen in quotation marks.

clue.text: Silly moment, getting rid of first new hired help

parts.note: a silly, as a noun, is a foolish person, an ass

indicators.note: getting rid of means discarding, and first says which occurrence of the letter goes

parts.note: an instant is a moment
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A daft moment when a new employee was dismissed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Silly' is a noun here, as in 'you silly'; only the first of the two Ns in the moment word goes.
explanation.definitionFit: An assistant is someone employed to help another, a paid helper.

clue.text: American who knows the ropes ties a liar in knots

indicators.note: something in knots is tangled up, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An experienced American binds up a dishonest person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'knows the ropes' sounds like experience; it is literal, as this performer works on ropes and the trapeze.
explanation.definitionFit: Aerialist is the American term for a trapeze artist or tightrope walker high above the ring.

clue.text: US writer making money here on book

parts.note: Ezra is a book of the Old Testament
the pound is the money here, in Britain

explanation.surface: An American author earning money from a book.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'A on B' puts A after B, so the money follows the book. 'Here' means Britain, where the paper is printed.
explanation.definitionFit: Ezra Pound was the American modernist poet behind the Cantos.

clue.text: Instrument from this country you said the French replicated

parts.note: the United Kingdom, where the paper is printed

indicators.note: said means spoken, so the word counts for how it is pronounced

parts.note: the letter U is pronounced like you
le is French for the, and replicated means it appears twice

explanation.surface: A musical instrument that a British speaker claims the French copied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'replicated' simply doubles the French article.
explanation.definitionFit: The ukulele is a small four-stringed guitar from Hawaii, a musical instrument.

clue.text: Pursue revolutionary, making brisk progress

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow them closely
a Trot is short for a Trotskyist

explanation.surface: Chasing a rebel, and getting on quickly.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogtrot is a gentle easy trot, a steady quick pace like a dog's.

clue.text: Gulls may be caught the day it begins

definitions.text: Gulls may be caught the day it begins

parts.note: surface reading: seabirds trapped
setter's reading: gulls are dupes, fooled on the opening day of this month

explanation.surface: Seabirds being trapped on the first day of some season.
explanation.walkthrough: A gull is also a dupe or easily fooled person; the first of this month is All Fools' Day, when people are tricked.
explanation.definitionFit: The month opens with Fools' Day on the first, when pranks catch out the gullible.

clue.text: Put together a written text when imprisoned

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something imprisoned is shut inside, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: MS is the abbreviation for manuscript
as means when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: Compiling a piece of writing while in jail.
explanation.definitionFit: To amass is to gather or accumulate, collecting things into one heap.

clue.text: Special language skill? Try to crack it

indicators.note: to crack something is to break into it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: art is skill, as in the art of persuasion
a go is a try or attempt

explanation.surface: Someone urged to attempt cracking a coded jargon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it' refers back to skill, so the try breaks into the skill.
explanation.definitionFit: Argot is the jargon or slang used by a particular group, such as thieves.

clue.text: Loutish one abroad appears to annoy worker

parts.note: un is French for one
to gall is to irritate
the worker ant is the standard crossword worker

explanation.surface: A boorish foreigner seems to irritate an employee.
explanation.definitionFit: Ungallant means discourteous, especially towards women, so boorish or uncouth behaviour.

clue.text: Director at first supports sentimental material

parts.note: twee means sweetly sentimental

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter of the word beside it

parts.note: the opening letter of Director

explanation.surface: A film director initially backs some mawkish material.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'supports' puts the director's letter underneath. Twee is a British word for cutesy or sickly sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: Tweed is a rough woollen cloth, a kind of fabric used for jackets.

clue.text: Damn pet disappeared!

parts.note: a dog is a common pet
gone means vanished

explanation.surface: An owner cursing because their pet has run off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Damn' looks like an exclamation of the owner; it is the definition, as a mild American curse.
explanation.definitionFit: Doggone is an American euphemism for damned, used as a mild oath or intensifier.

clue.text: Wire had damaged some leather

indicators.note: something damaged is broken out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A wire has scratched or torn a piece of leather.
explanation.definitionFit: Rawhide is untanned cattle skin, a kind of leather used for whips and ropes.

clue.text: Penniless person keen on culture

indicators.note: penniless means without a penny, and the penny's usual abbreviation is the letter dropped

parts.note: a party is a person, as in a third party

explanation.surface: A poor person who nonetheless loves the arts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Penniless' splits into penny plus less: the P comes off the front of PARTY.
explanation.definitionFit: Arty describes someone showily interested in the arts, so keen on culture.

clue.text: Went over again, to secure once more backing in special trade

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word is read from end to start
in places one piece inside the other
special means made to order, so the letters are put into an unusual arrangement

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
to retie is to fasten again

explanation.surface: Someone repeated a deal, securing it again with support in a specialised business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'special' is an unusual anagram signal, in the sense of specially made up; 'backing' attaches to the word before it, not to the trade.
explanation.definitionFit: To reiterate is to say or do something again, so went over again matches the past tense.
